en: Title: Kaumārasaṃhitā. Extent: 28 [verses].
Subject.
Tantra, folio 1a. Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa. [I bow to Him] who shines with two arms adorned with excellent golden great chains, and who possesses ten arms holding a citron and other objects.
I bow to that Gaṇeśa, whose crest is the moon, who has three eyes, whose complexion is like the vermilion of twilight, who is bent by the weight of his breasts, and whose body is well-proportioned;
above the neck he is a young elephant, while below it he is praised as a youth by the assembly of goddesses. He is complete with all weapons in his twelve excellent arms.
I bow to the primordial Elephant-faced One (Gajānana), who dwells below in the form of a woman.
On the beautiful slopes of the silver mountain, frequented by hosts of sages, surrounded by wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas),
and upon a peak resplendent with gold— [there he sits] amidst thousands of jeweled pillars.

Having arrived at the jeweled pavilion of Bhīti to behold the Great Lord (Maheśvara) seated upon the jewel-throne together with the Goddess, I, Brahmā, having prostrated before that ocean of mercy and joined my palms in reverence, praised the Supreme Lord. Brahmā said: Na... [The text provided ends here.]

Salutations to Lord Maheśiva, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss; salutations to the Guru of yogis, who is known through the Vedānta. Salutations to the moon-crested one, who bestows grace upon the world, and who is the very nature of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, [the source] of all beings.

[Page 2a] "Obeisance to the Self! (7). Having thus praised Mahādeva and bowing down again and again, the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees, spoke with a profound voice: (8). "Welcome! What is it that you desire, O Brahmā? Is it the creation, or perhaps some ritual act, or a hymn of praise? (9)

"I am not satisfied by this; what is the reason for your coming? To the Lord of Gods who had spoken thus, the Unmanifest Creator replied: "O Lord of Gods, O Master, you whose self is the universe, there is nothing here that should not be told by you. There is no vision other than that which comes through your grace. What [else could it be]?
The fruit for those like us is great; nevertheless, I desire to hear the secret that resides within the mind.

(12) The Lord of Gods must be worshipped by all the deities as well, for the Goddess Mahāmāyā is indeed the Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*), who consists of the entire universe. (12) By means of Māyā... [text continues]

"O Lord, you have previously stated that this entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is composed of the Supreme Brahman. Therefore, please tell me everything regarding the god Vighneśvara together with Śrīvidyā—the supreme [deity], as well as their mantras, yantras, and the characteristics of their preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa). || 13-14 ||

"Out of compassion, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, protect me! The Lord said: "Listen, O Brahmin, to the proper method for knowing Gaṇapati, the Lord—divine, the bestower of all sovereignty, the deluder of all worlds, and the means for achieving dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. [End of page 3a] All-successful...
This is the Siddhida [mantra]. ||16|| The Ṛṣi of Vidyāgaṇeśa is said to be Dakṣiṇāmūrti;

the metre (Chandas) is the Goddess Gāyatrī, and the presiding deity (Devatā) is Vidyāguṇeśvara. ||17|| Gaṃ is the seed-syllable (Bīja), and Hrīṃ is the power (Śakti); the application (Viniyoga) is for the purpose [of attainment]. [The mantra] is joined with the five seed-syllables, beginning with Umī...
Thus [ends] the six-limbed [rite]. 18. O Lord, Master of the Hosts of Vidyās, I shall now describe the meditation upon this [deity]:
the God who has the face of a lordly elephant, three eyes, and the moon as his crest-jewel;
below [whom] is a female form, with a body as red as vermilion. 19. [With] lofty breasts...

Adorned with ornaments of jewels rising like the sun, and decorated with tinkling *kiṅkiṇī* bells, a girdle, jeweled anklets, and bracelets; [he holds] a citron, a rosary, a bow of sugarcane, a trident, a discus, a lotus, a noose, a blue lotus, the tip of a grain of rice, his own teeth, and a jewel-pitcher. (20–21)

One should meditate upon Vighneśa, who is resplendent, holding a golden chain with his two beautiful hands adorned with bracelets, for the sake of accomplishing all goals. Having meditated thus, one should daily recite [the mantra] sixteen times in the morning; thereby, one attains all desires.
The Lord of Obstacles becomes pleased. (23) O wise one, I shall now declare the extraction of the mantra of Vighnarāja:
the *praṇava* (oṃ), the five seed-syllables, and the first section of the *vidyā*. (24) pṛ0 4a)

One should extract the second segment ending with the dative case of Gaṇapati; having uttered "Varada" twice, one should utter the third segment. Then, followed by "Sarvajanaṃ vaśamānaya," and saying "Svāhā"—this is the mantra of Gaṇeśa, which bestows all accomplishments.

26-27. One should receive this mantra, heard directly from the mouth of a true guru— [a mantra] which bestows wealth and grain, brings all people under one's influence immediately, promotes longevity, increases progeny, and destroys disease— to one who is endowed with virtues, a leader among scholars, devoted, and expert in mantras.

O Lord Gaṇapati, one should properly receive the knowledge of the Lord after having correctly understood it—being endowed with compassion, tranquil, and following the traditional lineage (pāramparya-krama).
One should receive it from both [the teacher and the disciple] for the sake of all accomplishment; for through the union of both, the secret [is revealed].
This has been stated [in verse 30]. Having gone into the presence of the guru with hands not empty [of offerings], one should please the guru and thereafter receive the supreme mantra. [31]
Thus ends the first extraction, titled "The Extraction of the Mantra of Vidyā-Gaṇeśa," within the *Vidyārahasya* section of the dialogue between Sadāśiva and Brahmā in the *Śrīkaumārasaṃhitā*.
(Folio 5a) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the *puraruścaraṇa* [the mountain-foot] at the mountain peak by the river.
On a riverbank, in a temple, or in a house;

in a solitary, secluded place, and especially in a clean location—sitting facing the east upon a seat made of khaṭvā-pāda wood, or even one made of kadamba wood, one should perform the recitation for the sake of attaining success in the mantra. [Anāsa...]
If a man should perform this recitation of the mantra while standing, his body will become exhausted and the deity will not be pleased with him. On a seat of darbha grass, the merit is onefold;
on a skin seat, it becomes eightfold. It is said that on a seat of kuśa grass (viṣṭara), the merit is sixteenfold, and on a ritual seat (karman), it becomes a hundredfold.

Having sat upon a pure seat and meditated with a concentrated mind upon the Guru (5), and then upon the Śrī-guru, the supreme guru, and the parāpara-guru, one should display the yoni-mudrā and offer salutations with one's head bowed (6). Then [one should worship] Gaṇapati, Durgā, and Kṣetrapāla...
One should place the [mantra] "Rasvatīm" on the two knees, preceded by the face, while bestowing skill. ||7||

Having worshipped the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti) with the mantra "Oṃ namas," one should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the seat (āsana) using the pure Mātṛkā. One should perform the placement of the root mantra (mūlamantra), beginning with the letter 'A' and ending with the letter 'Kṣa. Then, [one should place] the first section and the sections...
Beyond this, there are two [more]. (9) The supreme *kuṅkuma-nyāsa* consists of the three sections along with the *mātṛkā*.

Having thus performed the great *nyāsa*, one should then perform the *mantra-nyāsa*. (10) With undistracted mind, one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times; then, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*) as one-tenth of that amount. One should also [feed] the Brahmins...
[This concludes] the feeding of Brahmins. ||11|| O Brahmin, I shall now describe the libation (tarpaṇa) and the time for recitation (japa).

One should perform the recitation starting from the final watch of the night until the appearance of the sun. ||12|| Having taken fragrant water mixed with camphor, wine, and flowers, [one should place it] in a copper or bronze vessel.

Or else, [one may draw it] in a clay vessel. (13) A dot, a triangle, a hexagon, an eight-petaled and a sixteen-petaled lotus, three circles, and three squares—this is known as the worship-diagram (*pūjā-yantra*) of Brahmā, Vidyā, and Gaṇeśa. Having projected this diagram into water... (14)

One should satisfy the King of Goblins (Ghnarāja). Then, having performed the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) and meditated upon the Lord of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśvara), one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) at his head with an ablution from a jeweled pitcher. Thus, one should constantly perform this libation one hundred and eight times. At the conclusion of the libation, there is the food offering (naivedya).
One should offer a coconut and a bulbous root [of the plantain tree]. (17) Likewise, one should perform the recitation for the Great-Souled Vighneśa;
one should perform thirty thousand recitations of the mantra for its accomplishment.

(18) For the sake of propitiating Gaṇeśa, I shall describe the supreme fire-oblation (homa); one should prepare a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with the proper characteristics. (19) p. 7a) [End of page 7a]

[One should worship] you, who are adorned by the glory of the three [goddesses] as one; (19) having consecrated the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), which is one aratni in width and square on all sides, according to the prescribed rule, one should then perform the placement of the letters (lipinyāsa).
(20) One should arrange [the diagram consisting of] a dot (bindu), a triangle, a hexagon, and an eight-petaled lotus.

O Brahmin, having installed Viṣṇu in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should set aside a tenth part of that [offering]. Then, having sprinkled water around and strewn grass all around, one should prepare the ritual vessels and implements: the praṇītā vessel, the prokṣiṇī vessel, the ghee-pot, the dipping-spoon, and the offering-ladle within the interior of the pit.

(p. 7b) Having accomplished [the rite] according to the prescribed rule, one should then fill the *prokṣaṇī* vessel used for purification with water. Reciting the mantra "āpo devīḥ" (The divine waters), and having sprinkled [the materials] with those very waters while reciting the *tulajā* verses, one should perform the fivefold purification (*pañcaśuddhi*) after sprinkling [them] with the three [mantras]. Then...

Having brought [the water] while reciting the mantra "varuṇosi," one should place Varuṇa to the north of the fire and worship him thoroughly. Then, having performed the rites up to the consecration of the clarified butter (ājyasaṃskāra),
and having cleansed the sruk and sruva ladles, one should [place] the staff and the darbha grass both inside and outside for the deity.
One should cleanse [the site]. (26) Having laid the enclosing sticks (paridhi) around the fire and having offered the fuel-sticks into the fire, one should pray.
Then, having performed the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon the fire and meditated with a concentrated mind, (27) one should proceed.
Having invoked and worshipped the tongue [of fire], one should then worship the Mūrti;

thereafter, having performed the Ādhāra and the two Ājyabhāgas, one should fully worship Agni. Then one should perform the worship of the Pīṭha of the Lord Gaṇapati, after first worshipping the Ocean of Nectar and then the Kalpavṛkṣa.
Likewise, O Brahmin, there is the Island of Jewels (Maṇidvīpa), and further, the Island of Earth (Pṛthvīdvīpa).

In the center of the jeweled pavilion is a jeweled throne. Having worshipped the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti) and the Root-Nature (Mūlaprakṛti), as well as the qualities of Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas, which are intensely under the control of the Primal Force (Pradhāna).
[Page 8b] ...the suffixes -ktayaḥ ||31|| Having fully worshipped dharma and the others, as well as adharma and the others,

in their proper order, [one worships] the Self (ātman), the Inner Self (antarātman), and the Supreme Self (paramātman) ||32|| Having thus worshipped in this sequence the Lord, the Sovereign of Knowledge (Vidyāgaṇeśvara), with the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā... [and so forth].
One should invoke the Lord with jasmine flowers. One should meditate thus upon the Lord Gaṇeśvara, who has twelve arms, a reddish luster, a face like that of an elephant, and bestows boons;

whose form is beautiful, whose limbs are adorned with divine jewels, and who is the Lord of the hosts of Vidyās. Having thus meditated upon the Sovereign of the Gaṇas and having worshipped him according to the prescribed rite—
O wise one, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter to Kaṃ. 35.

O Brahmin, having offered oblations with the eight substances, one should again perform one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter (ājya), O wise one, according to the rule of twenty-two [repetitions]. The intelligent practitioner should perform these with the root mantra (mūlamantra) alone, excluding the attendant deities; however, in the case of the *puraścaraṇa* homa, the attendant deities are not excluded.

One should worship [the deity]. (37) Having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and recited the mantra sixteen times, one should perform the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścittāhuti*) preceded by the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*).
(38) With milk-rice, cakes, and waters like nectar, she whose resolve is for the propitiatory worship (*prasannapūjā*) [should offer these] to the virtuous ones.
One should offer the *vūla* (betel). Having worshipped again as before, one should perform the *puṣpāñjali* (handful of flowers), O Lord.
Then, having meditated upon the Blessed One, one should display the five mudrās.
Having rendered the one with attributes attribute-less, [one should contemplate] the embodiment of Being-Consciousness-Bliss through the left nostril.

One should not meditate upon the Lord within the heart-lotus; having attained the state of pure consciousness, one becomes endowed with a retinue. Having reached my heart-lotus, Vināyaka remains there. Having thus recited this, one should worship one's own self with perfumes and flowers.

Having united the fire with one's own self, one should utter this mantra: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, Ome! Come here, O Agni; protect my self. Having spoken thus, one should recite the root mantra according to its power. In this manner, one should prepare the maṇḍala.
If one is unable to perform this supreme rite oneself, I shall explain the means [to accomplish it].

(45) One should have a virtuous person—devoted to Gaṇeśa, learned in the Tantras of knowledge, and habituated to recitation—perform the recitation, libation, and fire-offering within the maṇḍala with devotion. (46) [One should also have] half a maṇḍala...

Or indeed that very same [rite], accompanied by four Brahmins including a Brahmin preceptor—if performed in the Kali age, what merit would it produce through recitation, libation, and fire-offerings? Or one may have them performed by others with devotion, increasing the count fourfold. Beginning at sunrise...
One should first perform the worship of the sacrificial priest (ṛtvij) and likewise the preceptor (ācārya) with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and other offerings.
Having worshipped them according to the rules with devotion, one should meditate upon the Lord of the Multitude of Sciences (Vidyāgaṇeśvara).
Then, one should feed them with milk-rice (pāyasa), fruits, cakes (apūpa), and various kinds of edible foods. 49-50. Ma.

Having bowed to them day after day, one should receive from them the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), betel, the recitation (japa), the libation (tarpaṇa), and the fire-oblation (homa), preceded by the giving of gifts. [The mantra for the gift is:
"I shall give the recitation, the libation, and the fire-oblation, which are the lords of all groups of sciences; O God, please accept them as your sacrificial fee."
"May [He] be gracious. ||52|| Having uttered this mantra, one should receive the fruit, the full fruit.
The Blessed One, being immediately pleased, grants all desires. ||53||

All rites are accomplished, and enemies stationed there are destroyed; from that time forward, one shall certainly become the lord of all hosts (Gaṇādhipati). Thus ends the second chapter on the rules for *puraścaraṇa* in the glorious *Kaumārasaṃhitā*. [Chapter 2]. [The section on] Worship...

I shall now proclaim before you the *dhānaka-vrata*; by mere worship, he who performs it will certainly become well-pleased and perfectly gracious. Furthermore, he who, during an eclipse of the moon or sun at Kāśī, performs the worship of a thousand *liṅgas*—and by that worship, the removal [of sins] through the mantra of the Lord of Obstacles (*Vighnapati*) and his own *vidyā*...

pṛ0 11ba) One attains the mountain-like [stability] through even a fraction of the art of worship. ||55|| This is the supreme secret, more secret than the secret, the most excellent; it is the cause of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation, and the means for subjugation.
||56|| It removes misfortune and disease, and destroys all enemies; by the final [syllable],...
Having risen from his seat, he should commence the act of worship (57). In a solitary, secluded place,
in a clean location, the wise one, having smeared it with cow dung and perfumed it with divine and excellent incenses (58), should sit upon a pleasant seat facing the east.
Or with a cheerful countenance, having performed the purification of the hands, one should then perform the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* (p.
12a). Having performed the *nyāsa* upon one’s own body, one should perform the *kuṅkuma-nyāsa*. [This should be done] on an image, or on a golden disc, or on a silver or copper one. 60. [Ātma...]

First, one should perform the worship; thereafter, the worship of the circle (cakrapūjā). Having meditated upon the jewel-throne (ratnasiṃhāsana), one should perform the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) as before. In the center, having invoked Vighneśa with the mantra "Gaṇānāṃ tvā," [one should worship] the host of sciences (vidyāgaṇa) endowed with all auspicious qualities.
"O Lord, while I perform worship here, please remain steadfast. || 62 ||
Having thus offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should display the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*).

(63) "O beings who are departing, those beings who are stationed upon the earth, and those beings who are creators of obstacles—may they perish by the command of Śiva! (64) "May those beings depart," [it is said]. (64)

One should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). Having first established a conch in a triangular or quadrangular mandala, one should fill it with scented water and display the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā).
Then, having invoked the sacred waters (tīrthas), such as the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, one should worship them.

O Brahmin, one should worship one's own self, as well as the materials for worship—namely the water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (argha), the water for sipping (ācamanīya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and so forth, O Lord. (67)

Having offered fragrant flowers, incense, and lamps (p. 13a), one should present the articles of worship, bringing milk mixed with the three sweets. Then, the pitcher worshipped with the ritual substances [should be honored] with fragrant flowers.
One should offer [the oblation] and then display the Dhenu-mudrā and the Yoni-mudrā (69).
One should perform the *amṛtīkaraṇa* (the rite of immortalization) while uttering that mudrā-mantra: "Haṃsaḥ śuciṣat" followed by "pra kṣad viṣṇoḥ" (70), and then "tryambakam."
Having recited the mantra originating from the nectar (Amṛtodbhava), and having worshipped again, one should honor the All-pervading Lord with nectar.
(71) Having filled five vessels—made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or coconut shell—with the nectar, one should worship the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnanāyaka). (72) One should worship...
One should worship [the deity] thirty times with clusters of flowers; then, having offered a bean-cake (māṣapūpa),

one should likewise offer water, drinks, and the like, along with milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with fruits, various colored varieties of cakes, and betel-leaf mixed with camphor, according to the prescribed ritual.
Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), one should worship the retinue.

At the tip of the triangle and at the root of the other tree, one should worship Ramā and the Lord of Ramā (Viṣṇu). At the root of the banyan tree to the south, one should worship Girijā and the Lord of Girijā (Śiva). Likewise, at the root of the holy fig tree (*aśvattha*) to the west, one should worship Rati and the Lord of Rati (Kāmadeva). And at the root of the *priyaṅgu* tree to the north, one should worship [the deity] upon the earth, O King.
Then, in the northwestern direction (Vāyavya), having worshipped four times the deity Gaṇādhipa, who bestows nourishment (Puṣṭideva),
one should worship the Śrīpādukā there. Holding nectar in the left hand and flowers in the other, one should thus worship the Lord.
Having worshipped the Great Goddess— who is the speech of delight and the speech of the mind— four times with the root mantra,
one should likewise worship Gaṇeśa four times with the root mantra.
Then, in the hexagon, one should worship the six pairs in Brahmā [the center] in due order. ||80||

[Having worshipped] Āmoda, Gaṇapa, Samṛddhi, Pramodaka, Kānti, Sumukha, Madanānvita, Durmukha, Madadravā, Vighnakara, Candravighna, and Makarṭaka— having worshipped these four times, [one worships] the Lord of the Gaṇas three times. (Page 14b, Verse 81)
One should worship with devotion Lakṣmī, Goddess Sarasvatī,
Kānti, Kīrti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi, respectively,
in the six corners of the fire [mandala] (82). Having worshipped [them] four times, one should worship Gaṇanāyaka three times outside the six corners (83).
One should worship Tovarā, Vasudhārā, Śaṅkhakā, Vasumatī, Padmanidhi, Indudayā, and Yastā;
thereafter, one should worship Mahāmāyā, Mahākālī, Mālinī, Mohinī, Bhoginī, Vidyā, and the Goddess. (84–85) One should fully worship...
One should conquer [the obstacles] in due order. Having worshipped the fourth enclosure, one should then worship the eight-petaled lotus:
Vakratuṇḍa Gaṇeśa, Ekadaṃṣṭraka, Mahodara Vighneśa, Lambodara Gaṇādhipa, Gajavaktra, and Vikata... [86–87].
Likewise, one should worship Vighnarāja and the Lord of the Gaṇas (Gaṇādhīśa) of smoky hue in due order.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa four times while reciting the mantra, one should likewise worship the goddess Anaṅgakusumā and Ānandamekhalā. Anaṅga... [p. 15b]
Having worshipped Madanā, Anaṅgamadanāturā, the goddess Anaṅgarekhā,
likewise Anaṅgaveginī, the goddess Anaṅgakuśalā,
and then Anaṅgamālinī— having thus worshipped Gaṇeśa four times with the root-mantra (mūlavidyā)— 90.

One should worship the Lord with the *śrīpātra* [offering vessel] and the retinue with other [vessels], using jasmine, pearls, divine flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and so forth. Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Worship," in the *Śrīkaumārasaṃhitā*. Now, [the fourth chapter...]

From that point, I shall fully explain the worship of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa-pūjana*). From the eight petals [of the lotus], one should worship Brahmā and the Bhairavas beginning with Sitāṅga. Sitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, the one known as Unmatta, Bhīṣaṇa, Kāpālī, and Saṃhāra—these are the eight Bhairavas. (93)

Having worshipped the sandals with devotion four times as before, one should thereafter worship the Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, in their proper order. [One should say: "I worship the venerable sandals of the goddess Brāhmī," and having thus worshipped them four times—

"By the root-mantra *ṇeśam*, may all the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī, together with their vehicles, weapons, and retinues, be worshipped. Thus one should worship from the first enclosure up to the ninth enclosure. Now follows the worship of the eight enclosures on the sixteen petals.

Now, I shall certainly proclaim this unsurpassed mantra. Within a triangle, a hexagon, and an eight-petaled lotus, one should then place an eight-cornered figure outside of that, which should be encircled by a *bhūpura* (fortress). In the center of the *bindu*, one should place Gaṇeśa, the Vedic seed-syllable (*bīja*) within the triangle. The mantra...

O Lord of Men, one should write the three syllables within the hexagon; the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), ending with *svāhā*, in the eight-petaled [lotus]; and all the syllables of the mantra, interspersed with the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*), within the eight-cornered [figure] and the city of the earth (*bhūpura*). One should likewise write the *vidyā* mantra together with the *tāraka* [syllable *oṃ*] upon the eight petals and the eight corners.

Having thus written [the mantra] according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the ritual installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). Having worshipped it with red flowers, one should offer worship for seven nights with milk-rice (*pāyasa*),
cakes, plantains, sweetmeats (*modaka*), betel leaves, and food offerings (*naivedya*), while reciting [the mantra] five thousand times.
One should hold this unsurpassed yantra in the right hand. Whether it be a king, his minister,
or others who depend upon him— men, women of various kinds,
as well as beasts and birds— they all come under one's control within seven nights.

[Page 17b] Doubt [regarding this]. Alternatively, one should draw the yantra on sandalwood paste mixed with saffron; having written the supreme yantra along with camphor, clarified butter, and honey, together with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), and likewise having performed the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), one should worship Gaṇeśa and recite [the mantra] eight thousand times.

O Great-Minded One, having taken that sandalwood and anointed one's own home with it, both men and women— upon seeing it and smelling its fragrance— become devoid of shame, their minds intoxicated with passion,
and they immediately fall under its influence; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.

Having brought rice flour mixed with ghee and sugar, one should fashion the form of the person to be subdued (*sādhya*) and cook it over a gentle fire. Then, having taken [the image], written the mantra, and placed it on the left arm of the *sādhya*, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times; at the conclusion of the recitation, one should consume it.

They come under his control by themselves until death; of this there is no doubt. One should draw the subjugation yantra with gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal. Whoever worships it and wears it, the three worlds shall come under his control. [One should also draw] the subjugation yantra upon other foodstuffs and edibles.

One should draw [the diagram], worship it, and having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, one should cause the subject to consume it, preceded by the ritual for the target. At that very moment, the person comes under one's control as long as the body exists. O Brahmin, having fastened the white [substance] consecrated with the mantra along with the yantra upon the target, one should go...

In the center of the diagram, a vajra should appear. Whatever mantra one recites while remembering [the deity], the accomplishment of that very thing occurs at that moment. Now, I shall describe various rites of attraction (ākarṣaṇa).
Having drawn the yantra as before, provided with the name of the person to be acted upon (sādhya),...

One should encircle all the seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*) with the seed-syllable of Māyā. At the end of the mantra, O Brahmin, one should write "sādhyaṃ ākarṣaya" (attract the target). One should worship the yantra for seven days according to the prescribed ritual as before, having honored it with red flowers and offered *siddhānna* (consecrated food).
One should give [the following]: one *prastha* of rice grains and half of that [measure] of split mung beans;
four fruits are prescribed for jaggery, and the same measure applies to coconut; black pepper should be one *muṣṭi*, rock salt half of that, cumin half of that, and ginger one *kuḍava*.
O Lotus-seated One, having combined ghee with an equal measure of cow’s milk and cooked it over a gentle fire, this is declared to be a perfected food (*siddhānna*).
It is truly like nectar and brings great pleasure to Vighneśa. When it is prepared, it attains a state equal to that which is to be accomplished.

There is no doubt that he will dwell [there]. Having drawn this yantra in its entirety upon a birch-bark leaf, one should bring a honey-pot and fashion the form of the person to be accomplished (sādhya).

Having fully worshipped the yantra, one should place it upon kuśa grass. Having fixed it upon a tall staff, one should heat its form over a lamp. One should constantly recite the mantra over that lamp while including the name of the person to be won over. Thus, the young woman, her mind agitated by passion, will quickly come to him.

One should take the dust from the left foot and inscribe the mantra upon it; joined with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), one should recite it eight thousand times. That [person] comes immediately; of this there is no doubt. Having approached Vighneśvara and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite... [sā]... *Note: The final fragment "sā" indicates the sentence continues in the source text.*

Having meditated [on this], one should mutter the mantra; it will surely come to pass, there is no doubt. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Śrī Kaumāra Saṃhitā. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the rite of paralyzing (staṃbhanam) which brings immediate results. Having drawn the yantra as before, preceded by the seed-mantra (vījamantra), [one should place] the letters of the mantra...

One should inscribe the short vowels in the middle of the seed-syllable (bīja). Having performed the stabilization of the vital breath (prāṇa-saṃsthāpana) and having joined it with the name of the one to be accomplished (sādhya), one should worship it for seven nights, especially with yellow flowers. One should write it on an iron or copper vessel, or on a birch-bark leaf (bhūrjapatra). Half...

One should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times daily at night. On the battlefield, one should draw the yantra and especially offer an oblation (*bali*); then the fourfold army, consisting of all its divisions, will become paralyzed.
[The same occurs] for those within a city, in the midst of an assembly, among the members of the assembly, and against locusts and other pests in the fields.

One should paralyze thieves on the path and even wild beasts; there is no need for further deliberation here. Having taken the urine of a bull once, until it falls upon the ground, one should then burn it into a solid mass (piṇḍa), especially on a Tuesday. From that ash, [one should prepare] the yantra...

Endowed with the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and having performed the consecration of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), one should worship it with yellow flowers. Having drawn [the diagram] with saffron, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times;
if one wears this *yantra* on the crest-lock (*śikhā*), there is no doubt that the world will be paralyzed. [This applies] in elephant battles and ram battles.
There is no mutual combat with weapons; by the mere application of the yantra, the opponent is paralyzed.
What need is there for much speaking? Listen to the secret, O Lotus-born One:
one should mutter the two words "ānaya" (bring) and "staṃbhaya" (paralyze), joined with the name of the person to be acted upon. One should perform the japa while paralyzing [the opponent].

In the rite of paralyzing, one shall paralyze [the enemy] by mere recitation alone; there is no doubt in this. Listen, O Brahmin, I shall describe the supreme method for the eradication of an enemy: having first drawn the yantra, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) within it, and all the syllables of the mantra [should be arranged] in the directions of the wind.

One should encircle [the deity] with the seed-syllable (*bīja*). Having performed the stabilization of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃsthāpana*), one should worship with black flowers. Having worshipped thus for nine nights, one should constantly recite [the mantra] eight thousand times. One should collect withered leaves and grass stalks that have arisen, as well as *nīlikā* from a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*).

One should take the root of *laṅgaratha-vartta*, the leaves of *karavīra*, and all the excrement (*viṣṭha*) at dawn (*svāsare*), during the rising of *kulika*. Having collected that ash in a black cloth using a mechanical device (*yantra-pūrvaka*) at the temple of Durgā-Kālī, one should [use] the bark of *vibhītaka*...

One should cast [the mantra] into the house of the enemy’s enemies. The enemy, together with his kinsmen, shall go to another land. Wherever it is placed, that [enemy] shall be eradicated in an instant. By the mere recitation of what is called the "word of eradication" (*uccāṭana*), eradication occurs immediately. Śa...

There is no doubt regarding these matters. Thus [ends] the fifth chapter of the Śrī Kaumāra-saṃhitā. Now, for the benefit of all the world, I shall proclaim the lotuses; specifically, that which bestows universal sovereignty upon kings, and by means of which all rites are accomplished immediately through the application of yantras and tantras.
I shall now describe the *homa* for the Lord, the pervasive Gaṇapati, whose knowledge is supreme.
Having prepared the *homa*-pit, it should be square and possess three ridges (*mekhalā*). One should make it one *aratni* in measure, or double that according to the specific rite.
For one's own sake, it should be one *aratni*; for the sake of others, it should be double. [The gods...]

If it is for the sake of others, one should perform it in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa); if for one's own sake, in one's own home. Having gathered much [material] in the pit, and having collected and purified it, O Brahmin, one should fashion the mouth [of the fire] according to the proportions of the cord (sūtra). One may also perform the rite of the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha) using the cord of the preceptor (ācārya-sūtra) itself within the pit.

Having meditated upon the lion-throne, one should perform [the rites] on the seat in due order. Having worshipped and meditated upon the Lord of the Gaṇas of Wisdom according to the previously mentioned path, one should invoke him with the mantra "gaṇānām tvā" and the other with the root mantra.
Having offered the arghya, pādya, and other services, one should worship him with perfumes and flowers. Da...

O Brahmin, one should offer incense, lamps, and coconuts; and having presented as an offering milk-rice (pāyasa), cakes, plantains, fruits, and so forth, the wise man should perform one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter (ājya).
There should be sixteen coconuts and twice that number of plantain fruits, along with sugar.
Having combined the eight substances— king-rice (rājapṛthuka), sweetmeats (modaka), honey, and clarified butter— with the syllables,
the wise one should perform the oblation until the syllables are exhausted. Then, having performed the worship of the nine elephants with devotion, [one attains] all desires.
Vighneśa becomes well-pleased and bestows [his favor]. One desiring sons obtains many sons;

one desiring wealth obtains an abundance of riches. One is released from shackles, and the sick are freed from great disease. O Brahmin, whatever one prays for when making the oblation, that is brought under control at that very moment. There is no doubt.
There is no need for hesitation; I speak this as the truth. One should perform ten thousand oblations with lotus flowers for the sake of prosperity.
A wise man should worship with jasmine flowers (jāti) to bring a king under his control, without a doubt. By offering oblations with *kuṭaja* and *campaka* flowers, one attains great sovereignty.

By offering an oblation with a *karavīra* flower, there is the destruction of enemies. O Brahmin, when oblations are made with red-colored flowers, silken garments and the like are obtained. By offering oblations of *māla* flowers (or *mīlala* flowers), ornaments and such are obtained. Through the homa of *japā* flowers, Vighneśa becomes well-pleased.

Having offered *kauśeya* flowers, one shall obtain success in yoga. By offering yellow flowers constantly, there shall be the paralyzing of the speech of enemies. Having offered *arka* flowers, the enemy shall suffer from fever and heat. Having offered *unmatta* flowers, [the enemy]— [Note: The source text appears to be incomplete.]

By offering parched grain (*lāja*) mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhura*), one becomes the subduer of all. By offering *kahlāra* lotus petals as an oblation, one brings even royal women under one's influence. By offering the powder of *daridrā*, there shall be the paralyzing of the three worlds. One should offer a pair of *dūrvā* blades immediately...
The destruction of all diseases occurs through a homa of ten thousand guḍūcī plants; even one who is dying returns to life.
By offering oblations of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter, the destruction of enemies is certain.
A wise person should offer one hundred and eight oblations to the Supreme Self (Paramātman); by means of the maṇḍala, cattle and grain will surely be obtained.
One who possesses prosperity, having performed the oblation to Vighneśa (Gaṇeśa), should thereafter commence everything;
without the oblation to Vighneśa, that rite shall become fruitless.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Śrī Kaumāra Saṃhitā, for the benefit of kings. 6. For the welfare of monarchs.

O Lotus-born one, I shall now describe that which consists solely of *homa*, which bestows sovereignty through mere oblation; it increases elephants, brings supreme prosperity to horses, increases progeny,
and likewise increases one's own self— all this shall come to pass, O Brahmin.
There is no doubt that [the result follows] from those oblations. Now I shall describe the daily oblation (*nityahoma*) exactly as it is; I will tell you:

having established the fire in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring only two cubits (*aratni*), one should place a single water-pot (*kumbha*) on the northern side of the pit, and one should fashion an image of Vighneśa.

Having performed the stabilization of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by means of the count of thirty-two finger-breadths, and having established Gaṇeśvara in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should worship him with perfumes and flowers and offer incense and lamps. Having prepared the food offering (*naivedya*) according to the rules with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), cakes (*apūpa*), and sweetmeats (*modaka*), one should present that to him in every way possible.
Then one should perform the *thājāta* oblation; having prepared the mouth of the fire on the altar and performed the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*),
one should invoke Gaṇādhīśa and offer the *arghya* and other gifts,
worshipping Vidyā-Gaṇapa according to the nine-fold enclosure (*navāvaraṇa*), followed by the oblation of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*).

Then, one should likewise perform one hundred and eight [offerings]. The preceptor, having first performed the rites up to the end of the *homa* according to the rules, should carry out the *homa* ritual with four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
O Brahmin, when the offering has been made with the eight substances one thousand and eight times, he should afterwards offer an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*).
The preceptor himself should perform [the rites] as previously described, preceded by the propitiation of Vighneśvara and the removal of obstacles.

Having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the *prasanna-pūjā*, one should worship Vighnarāja with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), cakes (*apūpa*), sweetmeats (*modaka*), water-offerings (*pānīya*), and various drinks. Then, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*).

One should display the *tvāpaśu* mudrā; having praised the Lord of the Gaṇas with hymns and meditated upon Him as the imperishable, pure consciousness, one should unite the Lord with the left nostril into the heart-lotus. Having worshipped oneself with flowers, one should mutter the mantra of the Lord according to one's capacity. As for the patron (*yajamāna*)...

At the conclusion of the *homa*, endowed with humility, he should perform a complete circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇā*) of Vighneśvara, the sacrificial pit (*homakuṇḍa*), and the preceptor (*ācārya*). Then, he should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor, and likewise always give to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) preceded by devotion; [the fee] for the preceptor should be double [that of the others].

One should daily feed the Brahmins equally, honoring them day after day, just as one honors the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Likewise, by means of the fire-oblation (*homa*), all objectives shall be accomplished; it directly increases longevity and destroys untimely death (*apamṛtyu*). All the aforementioned rites [are likewise effective].
Without doubt, it bestows fruit; it shall declare victory in battle and the destruction of all enemies.
At the time of battle, having constantly invoked Gaṇeśvara, one should prepare a sacrificial hall (homaśālā) consisting of sixty-four squares,
square in shape, and provided with four doors.

It should be provided with a canopy, mirrors, banners, plantain trees, and archways. In its center, there should be a sacrificial pit (homa-kuṇḍa) twice the size of the regular pit, equipped with three girdles (mekhalā), equal in measure to the cubit (aratni) of the performer on all sides.
One should place five jars in the northern part of the main jar. Vighneśa [should be installed]...

One should perform twice as many oblations as the daily fire-sacrifice (homa). Having performed the stabilization of the vital breaths (prāṇasaṃsthāpana), one should cast [the substance] into the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). One should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and the like, and honor it with incense and lamps.

Having offered the sacrificial food (*naivedya*) according to the prescribed rules, one should complete the rite of fire-oblation (*homa*). The preceptor (*ācārya*), having become pure and wearing a linen upper garment, should assume the tortoise posture (*kūrmasana*) and perform the recitation of mantras (*japa*) and other rites. Having established the fire in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), he should perform the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*) ceremony in due order.

Having made the mouth of the fire [of] the Āgamas, one should then, by means of the root-mantra (mūlavidyā), perform one thousand and eight oblations of clarified butter (ājya) according to the rule. Together with ten officiating priests (ṛtvij), when the eighth oblation has been offered,
one should constantly perform sixteen thousand homas in accordance with the prescribed ritual.

One should perform the recitation (*japa*) for each [deity] daily one hundred and eight times. On the western side of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), on ground adorned with rice grains, one should daily worship the planets (*graha*) starting from the Sun (*āditya*) in their proper order. One should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and cakes (*apūpa*) to Vighneśa (Gaṇeśa). Eight... [text continues]
On the fourth day, one should perform a libation (*tarpaṇa*) one thousand and eight times. One should have the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) recite the mantra one thousand and eight times.

One should offer three tens of thousands (*ayuta*) oblations with *vibhītaka* fuel-sticks. By performing the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) within the mandala in this manner, the enemy will surely flee through the grace of Vighneśvara.

It does not perish for him. One should constantly feed Brāhmaṇas and worship Vighneśa as well. At the conclusion of the *homa*, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and honor [the deities] with perfumes and flowers. One hundred *niṣkas* should be given to the preceptor (*ācārya*), and sixteen in succession to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). [This is the victory in battle as described...]
This [mantra] bestows immediate sovereignty, grants all divine powers, and causes all enemies to flee.
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the *Kaumārahitā*. Saṃvat 1942, Jyeṣṭha-kṛṣṇa 10. May there be auspiciousness!
